zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Supplied page subset; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The scan remains the authority for text and typography.

lines.note: Inchǔ is read from the printed headword, not the OCR's final x. Cacureta naca supplies the interior/hidden-place sense; the Portuguese clearly says Dentro do mosteiro, with two separate OCR letter confusions corrected.

The short continuation completes the preceding location gloss with ou varela. The first vowel has the form of italic a rather than the OCR o; the historical word itself is retained without replacement by a modern temple term.

Nodo identifies the throat sense of Incô. The gloss gives Garganta and gu ella; the unusual internal separation is retained. The terminal S. is upright apparatus, not part of the italic Portuguese definition.
The unaccented Inco is a separate bird entry, glossed Papagayo. It must not inherit the circumflex from the immediately preceding throat entry; the short row and final stop are fully visible.

The printed synonym begins Momi, although drinking would lead one to expect Nomi. The capital's multiple strokes support retaining this apparent source anomaly. Comer, & beber gives eating and drinking; the right-edge marks are discussed on the following line.

The example warns against making eating and drinking one's occupation. Retained printed Nã at the right edge. A loop-shaped, pen-like mark rises above it into the previous row; it may be an added o, but is not confidently identifiable as set type and is documented rather than silently inserted. Its crop extends upward to retain the complete mark for later inspection.

runs.text: vos entregueis todo a comer, & beber. S

lines.note: The translation completes the warning, telling the addressee not to devote himself wholly to eating and drinking. Singular todo is printed. The upright closing label has a visible comma after S rather than the OCR's full stop.

Michibiqu supplies the guiding sense of Indǒ. The Portuguese begins Guiar and particularizes its use; particularmente is supported by the visible lar sequence, correcting the OCR's dar sequence. The caron is retained.

runs.text: diz dos Bonzos que encaminhão as almas pera

lines.note: This continuation explicitly restricts the explanation to Bonzos guiding souls. Encaminhão and pera are preserved as printed; the latter is not modernized to para. The crop contains the complete accents and right-hand rule.

runs.text: o outro mundo com lhes fazerem exequias; &

lines.note: The Portuguese describes conducting souls to the other world through funeral rites. After exequias, enlargement shows both the upper dot and lower comma of a semicolon; the following ampersand belongs to this same physical row.

Comendações completes the description of rites and prayers. The paragraph mark begins the Japanese request Vaga xixiteno indǒua, whose in- is physically divided here; Vaga and xixiteno are not modernized from a reconstructed reading.

The initial dǒua completes indǒua from the preceding row. Qixouo and tanomi zonzuru form the deferential request, followed by Peço vos. The printed word joins and the caron are preserved rather than respaced by modern morphology.

runs.text: muito me encomendeis, & guieis pera a ſalua

lines.note: The translation continues the request for commendation and guidance toward salvation. Salua ends this row without a securely printed terminal hyphen; the following ção remains on its own physical row.
This short continuation completes saluação and specifies after death. It belongs to the request above, not to the following Indǒxa entry; the complete descender and full stop fit inside the crop.

runs.text: Bonzo que guia desta maneira as al-

lines.note: Indǒxa denotes the Bonzo who guides souls in the manner just explained. The Portuguese repeats that relation and breaks almas as al-; the caron and visible terminal hyphen are retained independently of adjacent entries.
Mas completes almas from the preceding row and is followed by the printed ampersand and c. abbreviation. The short continuation is a real physical row and must not be merged into its predecessor.

runs.text: Arroz em quanto eſtà na eſpiga.

lines.note: The capital and following letters read Ine. The definition concerns rice while still on the ear; quanto, not the OCR quamo, is supported by the visible n and t. Eſtà and the historic spacing em quanto are retained.

Two paragraph-marked rice examples begin here: Ineuo caru is glossed as reaping rice, and the second starts with Ine-. The clearly printed hyphen is retained because its uo continuation is on the following row.

runs.text: Debulhar o arroz, ou tiralo da

lines.note: Uo coqu completes the second example and is glossed as threshing rice or removing it from the ear. Coqu is a Japanese verb here, not a Portuguese word; the crop includes the long descenders in Debulhar and tiralo.
This isolated eſpiga completes the preceding definition. It remains an indented physical row with its final stop; no missing entry or new headword is inferred from the otherwise sparse line.
The principal forms Ine, uru, eta are printed together and glossed Dormir. This is the sleep verb, distinct from the preceding rice noun despite the matching initial spelling.

The capital Ine heads the noun meaning sleeping. The paragraph mark introduces Ineno varui fito, with l, offering the contrasting yoi fito on the next row; the two examples should be interpreted together, not as identical meanings.

Yoi fito supplies the alternative to the restless sleeper above. The Portuguese first describes the restless person and starts reuol-; its visible hyphen and the spacing of Japanese yoi fito are retained.

runs.text: ue muito no dormir, ou o contrario.

lines.note: The continuation finishes reuolue and explicitly adds ou o contrario, accounting for the opposed Japanese examples. The historical construction no dormir is preserved; it is not expanded into a modern paraphrase in the transcription.
Inemuri and its principal forms denote dozing. The whole Portuguese Toſquenejar, including its initial T, is italic; the OCR's isolated roman T is a font-boundary error, not a Japanese fragment.

Inen is glossed as a slight thought and accompanied by Sudeni vomô. The apparent semantic mismatch in the literal synonym is left in the source rather than repaired. The closing upright S. is separated typographically from the Portuguese gloss.

Cacomi, u provides the surrounding/encircling sense of Inhô. The definition says Rodear a companhando; the visibly separated a is retained rather than normalized to acompanhando. The circumflex is clear.

The line adds reverencing, then gives Inhô catgǒ ſuru. Enlarged comparison distinguishes the circumflex in Inhô from the small downward-pointing caron in catgǒ. Fa starts Fazer without a securely printed terminal hyphen.
Zer completes Fazer and the gloss describes great reverence and welcome. Printed agaſalhado is retained as an unusual form; it is not silently regularized to the more expected agaſalho.

Ingua is accompanied by Chinami fatçuru and mucui. The Portuguese begins Retribuição, physically divided as Retri-; the Japanese spelling gua and the synonym's tç are preserved rather than converted into modern romanization.

runs.text: buição, ou paga do que hum fez neste mundo,

lines.note: The definition describes repayment for what someone has done in this world. In neste, the draft's short s is retained rather than globally converting the st sequence to long ſ.

runs.text: ou em outro nacimento como cuidão os gentios.

lines.note: This continuation adds another birth and attributes the belief to the people the source calls gentios. Nacimento is retained as historical spelling. The note describes the dictionary's viewpoint, not an endorsement of its religious terminology.

The paragraph-marked example Inguano tçuqita fitode gozaru introduces an unfortunate person. All Japanese word joins remain as printed, including fitode; the Portuguese translation begins with the visibly divided Ho-.
Mem completes Homem and the gloss says completely unfortunate. This short continuation remains indented and separate from the next Inguai entry; the final stop is clear in the native crop.

Cazuno foca glosses Inguai as outside the number or reckoning. The Portuguese begins Fora do numero primeiro but divides primeiro after primei without a printed hyphen; one is not supplied merely because the word continues.

runs.text: ro, i, não ſer tido em conta. S.

lines.note: The continuation explains not being counted or taken into account. The upright S. closes the apparatus, while the Portuguese text remains italic. The printed i, is retained rather than expanded into a modern explanatory phrase.
Inguin is glossed as courtesy and reverence. The visible letters support Corteſia and reuerencia, correcting two OCR substitutions; the long ſ in the former is not changed to modern short s.

The example inguinna fito illustrates a courteous person. Homem is visible despite worn ink, correcting Honem. Vt and its following comma are italic apparatus; the example's lowercase initial remains as printed.

Inguinni and Inguinſa are the adverbial and nominal companions of the preceding courtesy adjective. This entirely Japanese row has no Portuguese gloss to invent, and the long ſ in the second form is retained.

runs.text: Iogo, ou exercicio q̃ fazem os moços cõ

lines.note: Ingi is explained as a game or exercise performed by boys. The damaged but legible moços, not meços, is supported by the round vowel and cedilla. Both abbreviation tildes in q̃ and cõ are retained on their printed carriers.

runs.text: armas, paos, &c. ou às pedradas. Vt,

lines.note: The definition lists weapons, sticks and stone-throwing, then begins the Japanese example with In. The example continues as giuo on the next row without a securely printed hyphen; the accent in às remains Portuguese.

Giuo ſuru completes Ingiuo ſuru from the preceding physical row. Its separation here is purely lineation; neither a new entry nor an extra space is inserted into a hypothetical continuous-text reading.

The principal forms Ini, uru, inda are glossed as going away or returning. The historical verb forms and the reflexive Portuguese spellings Irſe and tornarſe are retained; there is no reason to regularize them from modern conjugation.

runs.text: Fotoque no tempo que era homem ordina-

lines.note: In-i is a distinct hyphenated headword. The Portuguese explanation embeds Fotoque and describes the time when that figure was an ordinary human; the embedded term is a font-review candidate, unlike the headword itself.

The short continuation completes ordinario and compares the person to other people. The physical row, indentation and final stop are retained; no doctrinal interpretation is added to the canonical text.

The damaged opening letters are read as Inixiye, supported by their surviving strokes and the past-time gloss, not the OCR mixiye. The visible space in an tiguamente and the paßado ligature are retained; capitalization is less secure because the initial is worn.

The paired expression repeats Inixiye with ima, meaning formerly and now. Its damaged beginning agrees with the preceding entry rather than OCR auixiye. The comma separates the temporal terms, and the first letter's case remains a minor scan uncertainty.

Inja and Cacururu fito describe a withdrawn person. Enlargement shows a long-s-plus-s ligature in Peßoa, rather than a single ſ. The close join in Peßoaretirada is retained from the aligned draft; apar- visibly continues on the next row.

runs.text: tada do mundo, & trafego delle. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The faint initial t completes apartada across the break. The heavily abraded vowel in delle is supplied from compatible remnants and the surrounding phrase about worldly business; this remains a localized uncertainty. The closing Itẽ has a visible comma, not a full stop.

runs.text: Peßoa que folga de eſtar recolhida, & foge quã

lines.note: A second sense describes someone who enjoys seclusion and avoids worldly activity. The printed Peßoa ligature and quã abbreviation are retained; quã continues as to on the next row without an added hyphen.

runs.text: to pode trafego, & negocios como corteſias,

lines.note: To completes quanto, and the explanation lists business and social courtesies. The printed syntax lacks an expected modern preposition or article before trafego; none is supplied merely to improve the sentence.
The short continuation adds visits and ends with the ampersand-plus-c. abbreviation. It remains its own indented row and is not mistaken for a separate entry or swallowed by the following Injen crop.

runs.text: Mandado do Rey que eſtà ja retirado

lines.note: Injen is an order from a ruler already retired from government. The initial e in eſtà is clearly visible after que and is restored; the OCR's stà omits a printed letter. The grave is retained.

This continuation completes the qualification that the ruler is retired from governing. Gouerno is left in its historical spelling; the short row and its final punctuation are fully included in the crop.

Cacureta coto gives the hidden-matter sense of Inji. The Portuguese gloss and Vt introduce the example on the following row; the apparatus is italic, while the Japanese headword and synonym remain roman.

The example says there is no hidden matter that fails to become apparent. Its negative forms arauarezuto and naxi are retained, together with the visible mark in yǔ; they are not rewritten into modern Japanese spelling.

runs.text: couſas eſcondidas por derradeiro ſe deſcobrem,

lines.note: The translation explains that hidden things are eventually discovered. Por derradeiro is historical phrasing, and the printed spaces around ſe are retained rather than redistributed from modern sentence structure.
This short continuation adds that such matters become known. The initial ampersand and final stop are printed, and the row belongs to the preceding maxim rather than to the separate Inji entry below.

This second Inji entry concerns what the dictionary calls disreputable carnal pleasures. Its moral description is part of the source, not a reviewer judgment; the headword must remain separate from the hidden-matter entry.
Injo and Cacuredocoro identify a place of retirement. The Portuguese definition begins Lugar onde hum ſe re-; the terminal hyphen is visible and is not confused with the nearby column rule.

runs.text: tira, & aparta dos negocios, & trafego do mũdo.

lines.note: The continuation completes retira and describes separation from worldly business. The abbreviation in mũdo has its tilde on u, and the ampersands remain as printed rather than expanded into words.

runs.text: Guiar as almas no outro mũ-

lines.note: Injô and Fiqitoru refer here to guiding souls in the other world. The first Portuguese letter is a capital G, giving Guiar, not OCR Ouiar. The headword's circumflex and the abbreviation in mũ- are independently retained.

The gloss adds saving the souls, then gives Raicǒ injô. The opposite directions of the two vowel marks are visible: caron in Raicǒ, circumflex in injô. The translation begins Vir ao on this physical row.
The continuation describes coming to meet and save these souls. The final S. is upright apparatus. Deſtas and ſalualas are preserved in historical spelling, without importing modern word division.
Injocu is explained with the repeated Japanese Xitone xitone and the Portuguese Colchoẽs. The tilde belongs over e in the vowel sequence, not over o; the definition continues onto the next row.

runs.text: ſemelhante que ſe estende na cama.

lines.note: This continuation describes something spread on a bed. The printed estende sequence is retained from the locally aligned draft rather than globally regularizing every st ligature into long-ſ spelling.

Inju is the female-tree entry, with Megui following i,. Vt introduces a contrast with a male term on the next row. Megui is an ordinary Japanese synonym here, not a word embedded in Portuguese for font toggling.

The opposite term looks like printed yǒſu: the tall undescended letter supports ſ, although the context would suggest a male-tree word with j. This apparent source anomaly is retained; the Portuguese clearly contrasts male and female trees.

Mea completes femea and is followed by i, with a visible comma, then Vogui, megui. These are ordinary Japanese equivalents of the male/female pair and are not separately marked as embedded typeface terms.

This homographic Inju is glossed by Cazu and Numero de couſas. The meaning is number or count, unrelated to the adjacent tree and religious-office senses; the separate row and full stops are retained.

runs.text: Bonzo que he como ſuperior, ou dono dal-

lines.note: Another Inju denotes a Bonzo who is superior or proprietor of a small religious establishment. The ending reads dal-, not the OCR dol-; the following gũa completes the contraction on the next physical row.

runs.text: gũa ermida, ou Tera particular onde mora.

lines.note: Gũa completes dalgũa, with the tilde on u. Tera occurs inside the Portuguese description of the particular establishment where the Bonzo lives, so it is an embedded Japanese term suitable for human font review.

Inmon is paired with Votozzure tô and glossed as a message or letter. The synonym's damaged t is reconstructed from its surviving stroke and the coherent phrase, not modernized to a different spelling; the circumflex is retained.

The printed first vowel in olguem is rounded and lacks the right-hand stroke of nearby italic a, so the anomalous olguem is retained rather than corrected merely by expectation. The example begins Inmonni azzu-, with its visible hyphen.

runs.text: Recebi voßa carta, ou recado. S

lines.note: Caru completes azzucaru. The translation acknowledges receipt of a letter or message, retaining the voßa ligature. The terminal S, is upright apparatus with a comma, not part of the italic gloss.

runs.text: Dentro da Tera, ou do circuito della.

lines.note: Innai means within the Tera or its enclosure. Tera is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation, rather than a headword or standalone example, and is therefore a valid typeface-review candidate.

runs.text: Cuidar couſas de goſtos ſenſuaes, ou

lines.note: The first Innen entry concerns sensual thoughts. The Portuguese begins with a visibly lowercase cuidar, retained even though a modern editor might capitalize it. Goſtos and ſenſuaes remain in their printed historical forms.
This short continuation restates the sense as carnal thoughts. It closes the first Innen entry and must not be merged with the next homograph, whose meaning is different.

The damaged initial is read as I in Innen, not the OCR e. The gloss gives cause or origin; the punctuation immediately after the headword has a clear descending tail and is retained as a comma rather than a period.

runs.text: El Rey velho que renunciou ja o

lines.note: Inno goxo denotes the old ruler who has relinquished his reign. Renunciouja is closely joined in the scan and retained from the aligned draft; the Japanese goxo remains unnormalized.

The continuation completes the reign reference, then adds another sense: the ruler's palaces. The paragraph mark and Item punctuation are retained, and the Portuguese paços is not confused with passos.

Innǒ is glossed as the scrotal sac. The downward-pointing caron is distinct from adjacent circumflexes; the anatomical definition is transcribed without euphemistic alteration or supplementary medical interpretation.

The headword clearly reads Inochi, not OCR mochi, and is glossed Vida. Inochiuo noburu begins the first example. The Portuguese fragment Di- appears in upright type in this cramped position and is retained as roman rather than automatically italicized.
Latar completes Dilatar, extending life. The next examples are Inochiuo iquru and na-garayuru; the visible hyphen after na is retained, while the Japanese alternatives remain roman.
Garayuru completes the previous verb. The Portuguese is Viuer, with u rather than the OCR t; the paragraph mark then introduces Inochiuo tatçu, taking someone's life.

The Portuguese Tirar begins with the same italic capital style as the rest of the gloss; the draft's isolated roman T is removed. Another paragraph mark starts Inochiuo ſu-, whose verb continues below.

runs.text: Deſprezar a vida, ou dala ſẽ doo.

lines.note: Tçuru completes ſutçuru. The gloss describes disregarding life or giving it without regret; the tilde in ſẽ and the double o in doo are preserved rather than modernized.

This paragraph-marked example reads Inochiuo taſucaru and is glossed Saluar a vida. The original construction is retained without changing its particle or verb on modern grammatical grounds. A visible space follows the paragraph mark.

The repeated object reads Inochiuo, correcting the OCR Iuochiuo. The damaged b in tabô remains compatible with the expected life-preserving verb, and the circumflex is visible; this small worn-letter reconstruction is noted as uncertain.

The continuation completes poupala and introduces Inochiuo voximu. Initial v and internal x are normal source spellings and are not modernized; the grave in the Portuguese dò is independently retained.
The gloss completes the feeling about one's life, then introduces Inochiuo caronzuru. The Japanese verb concerns treating life lightly; the Portuguese translation begins the visibly divided Fa-.
Zer completes Fazer and the gloss explains making little of life. The next paragraph begins Inochiuo ſu-, with the printed hyphen preserved rather than joined to the following row.

Guru completes the printed ſuguru, glossed Paßar a vida. This historical verb form is not replaced by a more familiar modern expression. The next phrase starts Inochino ca-, with its own visible hyphen.

Guiri completes caguiri and is glossed as the limit of life. A final paragraph mark and Inochiuo begin an example that continues beyond this page. The lower-right caguiri is separate catchword furniture, not an extra body continuation here.
